claims.feature: excellence only about half the time
claims.claim: GPT-4 and Claude can produce excellent literary summaries, but only about half the time.
claims.source: Subbiah, Zhang, Chilton, McKeown — 'Reading Subtext: Evaluating Large Language Models on Short Story Summarization with Writers' (TACL 2024)
claims.quote: excellent summaries, but only about half the time

claims.claim: Nearly all writers noticed a single default voice in the generations, bland and elementary in its language.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: bland and somewhat elementary in its use of language

claims.claim: Several writers compared the suggestions to those of a novice fan-fiction writer, pitched at an implicit audience of internet users.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)

claims.feature: genre collapses to its most worn trope
claims.claim: The model pushed a fantasy story toward warrior-hero-versus-invaders and treated genre as its dominant trope.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: fantasy is high fantasy, science fiction is robots and spaceships

claims.claim: A lesbian romance kept receiving suggestions to add a male character; unspecified gender defaulted to a male voice.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: kept suggesting that she insert a male character

claims.feature: characters are not allowed to be mean
claims.claim: Safety tuning made the system reluctant to generate people doing mean things, flattening conflict.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: seemed very reluctant to generate people doing mean things

claims.feature: exemplar names leak into every story
claims.claim: Prompt exemplars containing 'Sarah' caused the system to try inserting a Sarah into every participant's story.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)

claims.claim: All participants complained that the model's understanding of their story was superficial, worsening with length.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: understanding seemed superficial if not entirely absent

claims.claim: The model offered only simple, sensible metaphors where writers wanted complex or not-quite-sensible ones.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: sometimes one wants metaphors to be complex, or not quite sensible

claims.claim: Suggestions slid easily back into tropes and repetition, a named system limitation.
claims.source: Ippolito, Yuan, Coenen, Burnam — 'Creative Writing with an AI-Powered Writing Assistant: Perspectives from Professional Writers' (arXiv 2022)
claims.quote: Suggestions too Easily Revert to Tropes and Repetition

claims.claim: Writers reported the model writing the same story over and over with a new surface, regardless of prompt.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Padmakumar, Brahman, Muresan — 'Creativity Support in the Age of Large Language Models: An Empirical Study Involving Emerging Writers' (arXiv 2023)
claims.quote: writes exactly the same story over and over again

claims.claim: The system autocompletes toward the most obvious version of any request, the opposite of good fiction.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Padmakumar, Brahman, Muresan — 'Creativity Support in the Age of Large Language Models: An Empirical Study Involving Emerging Writers' (arXiv 2023)
claims.quote: autocompletes with the most obvious version of whatever you ask for

claims.claim: The model tells rather than shows and cannot write real scenes with realistic dialogue and detail.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Padmakumar, Brahman, Muresan — 'Creativity Support in the Age of Large Language Models: An Empirical Study Involving Emerging Writers' (arXiv 2023)
claims.quote: much better at telling than showing

claims.claim: Every ending arrived as a stated lesson, uplifting and didactic whether or not the story wanted it.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Padmakumar, Brahman, Muresan — 'Creativity Support in the Age of Large Language Models: An Empirical Study Involving Emerging Writers' (arXiv 2023)

claims.feature: binary tone; no nuance between happy and fatalistic
claims.claim: The model resists ambiguity and treats any story that is neither happy nor wholly fatalistic as flawed.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Padmakumar, Brahman, Muresan — 'Creativity Support in the Age of Large Language Models: An Empirical Study Involving Emerging Writers' (arXiv 2023)
claims.quote: The story must be either happy or entirely fatalistic

verdicts.trueWording: GPT-4 and Claude can produce excellent summaries, but only about half the time.
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (arxiv.org/html/2403.01061) reached; byline Subbiah/Chilton/McKeown confirmed. Quote is verbatim in the Introduction's key-findings list ('Our key findings are: 1.) GPT-4 and Claude can produce excellent summaries, but only about half the time.'). Every limb holds: the models evaluated are GPT-4, Claude-2.1 and Llama-2-70B on 25 unpublished short stories judged by their own authors, so 'literary summaries' is faithful to the setting.

verdicts.trueWording: Nearly all the writers noticed a 'default' voice, bland and somewhat elementary.
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (2211.05030) reached; byline Ippolito/Yuan/Coenen/Burnam confirmed. Section 7.1: 'Nearly all the writers noticed that there seemed to be a “default” voice to the language model’s generations, one that was bland and somewhat elementary in its use of language.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported. The claim drops only the hedge 'somewhat'.

verdicts.trueWording: Multiple participants compared Wordcraft's suggestions to a novice fan fiction writer.
verdicts.note: Both limbs sit in adjacent sentences of Section 7.1: 'MT described this as the AI having an implicit target audience: internet users. Multiple participants compared Wordcraft’s suggestions to those of a novice fan fiction writer.' Quote verbatim. Attribution nuance worth knowing: the fan-fiction comparison is 'multiple participants' (matching 'several writers'), while the internet-users audience is one writer's (MT's) description of the same default voice; the page orders the two the other way round from the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: Wordcraft insisted on pushing the story toward a warrior hero fighting invaders.
verdicts.note: Section 7.2: YW's premise deliberately made the heroes cartographers and builders rather than warriors, 'but Wordcraft insisted on pushing the story toward the well-worn trope of a warrior hero fighting back enemy invaders.' The quoted genre line follows immediately and verbatim, attributed to NG: 'For Wordcraft, “fantasy is high fantasy, science fiction is robots and spaceships”'. Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: The system kept suggesting she insert a male character; unspecified gender defaulted male.
verdicts.note: Section 7.2: 'NG noted the difficulty in writing a story with a lesbian romance plot–the system kept suggesting that she insert a male character or that she have the female protagonists talk about friendship. WT found that when no gender was specified, Wordcraft tended to default to a male voice.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported, each by a named participant.

verdicts.trueWording: The software seemed very reluctant to generate people doing mean things.
verdicts.note: Section 8.2: the page itself supplies the safety-tuning causation — LaMDA was finetuned on data 'labeled by human annotators as safe and sensible', and 'This intentional biasing is a strength in some respects… but it can also be limiting. For example, MT found that “the software seemed very reluctant to generate people doing mean things”'. Quote verbatim. The 'flattening conflict' limb is the paper's own consequence in its wording: 'a literary world where no character is ever mean is unlikely to be a very interesting one.'

verdicts.trueWording: Wordcraft attempted to insert a character named 'Sarah' into every participant's story.
verdicts.note: Section 7.3: 'several of Wordcraft’s controls were implemented with exemplars that contained the name “Sarah.” This had the unintended consequence that Wordcraft attempted to insert a character named “Sarah” into every single participant’s story.' Quote verbatim including the curly apostrophe; both limbs (exemplar cause, universal effect) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: All participants complained the model's understanding seemed superficial if not absent.
verdicts.note: Section 7.5 ('Model’s Natural Language Understanding is Superficial and Insufficient'): 'All participants complained that the language model’s understanding seemed superficial if not entirely absent.' Quote verbatim. The length limb is supported two sentences later: 'This problem got worse, the longer the story,' with the 1024-token LaMDA sequence limit given as the technical cause.

verdicts.trueWording: Wordcraft generally suggests simple and sensible metaphors.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the exclusivity 'only' — the page says Wordcraft 'generally' suggests simple and sensible metaphors, not that it offered nothing else
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in Section 8.2, attributed to JM: 'Wordcraft generally suggests simple and sensible metaphors; but sometimes one wants metaphors to be complex, or not quite sensible.' The wanting-complex-metaphors limb is fully supported (JM's generic 'one wants' covers the claim's 'writers wanted'). Only the quantifier fails: the claim's 'offered only simple, sensible metaphors' is exclusive where the page is merely typical ('generally').

verdicts.trueWording: Section 7.2 heading: 'Suggestions too Easily Revert to Tropes and Repetition'.
verdicts.note: The quote is verbatim as the title of Section 7.2, inside the paper's numbered list '7 System Limitations Experienced by Participants' — which supports the claim's 'a named system limitation' limb precisely: it is a named subsection of the limitations section, not an incidental remark.

verdicts.trueWording: It writes exactly the same story over and over with a new skin on it.
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (2309.12570) reached; byline Chakrabarty/Padmakumar/Brahman/Muresan confirmed. Table 8 (participant feedback on AI weaknesses), SH: 'It feels oftentimes as if it writes exactly the same story over and over again with a new skin on it, rather than even generating a different feeling arc given even vastly different prompts. It has one narrative that it knows how to write, and that’s all it does.' Quote verbatim; 'new surface' = 'new skin', 'regardless of prompt' = 'given even vastly different prompts'. The plural 'writers' is carried by neighbouring entries in the same table (ATK on redoing rather than building, NM on paragraphs that 'always feel similar').

verdicts.trueWording: It effectively autocompletes with the most obvious version of whatever you ask for.
verdicts.note: Table 8, MC: 'A teacher once told me that the best fiction writing is the opposite of autocomplete - this system, on the other hand, effectively autocompletes with the most obvious version of whatever you ask for.' Quote verbatim; the claim's 'the opposite of good fiction' limb is the page's own antecedent clause about the best fiction writing.

verdicts.trueWording: It is much better at telling than showing — reversing the writing maxim.
verdicts.note: Table 8, MC: 'It still relies on cliches, and it is much better at telling than showing - reversing the writing maxim. It can’t effectively write real scenes with realistic dialogue and details, but can generate general sketches based on well-known tropes.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported nearly word for word (the claim's 'cannot' compresses the page's 'can’t effectively').

verdicts.trueWording: All the endings were 'Here is the lesson learnt'; uplifting and didactic.
verdicts.note: Table 8, under 'Overly Moralistic and Predictable Endings', MG: 'It seems that the ChatGPT is very moralistic - all the endings it gave me are all very much “Here is the lesson learnt”.ChatGPT seems very into being uplifting and didactic to the audience and not every short story wants to do that'. Quote verbatim. Every limb holds, including the universal 'Every ending' (page: 'all the endings it gave me') and 'whether or not the story wanted it' (page: 'not every short story wants to do that').

verdicts.trueWording: Unwillingness to accept nuance; anything that strays is a flaw.
verdicts.note: Table 8, under 'Lack of Nuance Subtext or Symbolism', SH: 'Its unwillingness to accept nuance. The story must be either happy or entirely fatalistic and the model finds that anything that strays is a flaw in the work.' Quote verbatim; 'resists ambiguity' = 'unwillingness to accept nuance', and the treats-as-flawed limb is the page's own trailing clause.
